subject: Physics
title: Thermal Equilibrium
description: The state reached when two or more objects in contact reach the same temperature, with no further net transfer of thermal energy between them.
learning_objectives: Define thermal equilibrium
Explain why thermal energy flows from hotter to cooler objects until equilibrium is reached
Describe how thermal equilibrium is used in practical temperature measurement
explanation: Thermal equilibrium is the state reached when two or more objects that are in thermal contact (able to exchange thermal energy) reach the same temperature, at which point there is no further NET transfer of thermal energy between them. When two objects at different temperatures are placed in contact, thermal energy naturally flows from the hotter object (with particles of higher average kinetic energy) to the cooler object (with particles of lower average kinetic energy), through processes such as conduction, as faster-moving particles transfer some of their kinetic energy to slower-moving neighbouring particles through collisions; this net flow of energy continues until both objects reach the same temperature, at which point their particles have the same average kinetic energy, and although individual particle collisions and energy exchanges continue to occur in both directions, there is no longer any NET transfer of energy from one object to the other overall. Thermal equilibrium is a foundational concept used throughout thermal physics, and underlies the practical operation of thermometers, which are designed to reach thermal equilibrium with whatever they are measuring, so that the thermometer's own final temperature accurately reflects the temperature of the object or substance being measured.
key_concepts: Same temperature; no further NET thermal energy transfer
Energy flows hot -> cold until equilibrium
Basis for how thermometers work

definitions.definition: The state reached when two or more objects in thermal contact reach the same temperature, with no further net transfer of thermal energy between them.

worked_examples.problem: A hot metal spoon is placed into a cup of cooler tea. Describe what happens to the temperatures of the spoon and the tea over time, and explain why this process eventually stops.
steps: Initially, the spoon is at a higher temperature than the tea, so thermal energy flows from the spoon (hotter) to the tea (cooler) through conduction.
As this energy transfer continues, the spoon's temperature decreases while the tea's temperature increases.

This process continues until the spoon and the tea reach the same temperature (thermal equilibrium), at which point there is no longer a net flow of thermal energy in either direction, so both temperatures stop changing.
worked_examples.answer: The spoon cools down and the tea warms up until they reach the same temperature (thermal equilibrium), after which both temperatures remain constant, since there is no further net transfer of energy between them.

practical_applications: The operation of thermometers, which rely on reaching thermal equilibrium with the substance being measured
Designing insulation and heating/cooling systems, understanding how objects approach thermal equilibrium with their surroundings
Food safety and cooking, understanding how quickly food reaches thermal equilibrium with its environment (e.g. cooling or heating)
common_mistakes: Assuming thermal energy transfer stops instantly once two objects touch, rather than continuing until they reach the same temperature
Assuming thermal equilibrium means all particle motion stops, rather than meaning the average kinetic energies (temperatures) become equal
misconceptions: That reaching thermal equilibrium means no further energy exchange occurs at all between the particles of the two objects — at thermal equilibrium, individual particles are still constantly colliding and exchanging small amounts of energy back and forth in both directions; what stops is the NET (overall) flow of energy in one particular direction, since the exchanges in both directions become balanced once the average kinetic energies (temperatures) are equal.
tips: Remember thermal equilibrium is defined by equal TEMPERATURE (average kinetic energy per particle), not necessarily equal total thermal energy, especially if the two objects have very different sizes or masses.

basic: State the condition, in terms of temperature, that defines thermal equilibrium between two objects.
intermediate: Explain why a thermometer must be given time to reach thermal equilibrium with a substance before an accurate temperature reading can be taken.
advanced: Two objects of very different mass reach thermal equilibrium with each other. Explain why they have the same temperature, but not necessarily the same total thermal energy.

exam_questions: Explain, in terms of particle kinetic energy, why thermal energy flows from a hot object to a cooler object in contact with it, and why this flow eventually stops.

basic: Both objects are at the same temperature.
intermediate: The thermometer itself must exchange thermal energy with the substance and reach the same temperature as it (thermal equilibrium) before its own reading (which reflects the thermometer's own temperature) accurately represents the temperature of the substance being measured; if read too soon, the thermometer may not yet have fully equalised with the substance, giving an inaccurate reading.
advanced: Temperature reflects average kinetic energy per particle, which becomes equal for both objects at thermal equilibrium, regardless of their size or mass; total thermal energy, however, depends on both this average energy per particle AND the total number of particles present, so the more massive object, having many more particles, would have a greater total thermal energy than the less massive object, even though both have reached the same temperature.
exam: In the hotter object, particles have a greater average kinetic energy than in the cooler object; when the two are in contact, faster-moving particles in the hotter object collide with and transfer some kinetic energy to the slower-moving particles in the cooler object, more often than the reverse, producing a net flow of thermal energy from hot to cold; as this continues, the average kinetic energies of both objects' particles become closer together, and once they become exactly equal (the same temperature), the energy transfers in each direction balance out exactly, and there is no further net flow of energy, defining thermal equilibrium.

summary: Thermal equilibrium is reached when two objects in contact reach the same temperature, with no further net transfer of thermal energy between them. Energy flows from hotter to cooler objects until this equilibrium is reached, underlying the operation of thermometers.
revision_notes: Thermal equilibrium: same temperature, no further NET energy transfer
Energy flows hot -> cold until equilibrium reached
Basis for thermometer operation
